sections.title: Preliminary Design
sections.summary: Preliminary design begins with terrain reconnaissance and an office study collecting existing information: USGS topographic and geologic maps, USDA soil surveys, well logs, air photos, and construction records from nearby structures. Results inform the subsurface exploration plan. A field reconnaissance with the bridge engineer and design team should be scheduled to discuss foundation type alternatives.
sections.body: (pp. 29-30) Preliminary design activities include a terrain reconnaissance and an office study collecting existing information relevant to the project area. Sources of information include USGS topographic maps, geologic maps from USGS or state geology agencies, USDA soil survey maps, well logs from local water resource agencies, air photos, and construction records from nearby structures. The terrain reconnaissance should focus on understanding the geologic and geomorphic features (landforms) likely present at the project site. This information should be used to plan the subsurface exploration program. A field reconnaissance should be scheduled with the bridge engineer and design team to discuss foundation type alternatives and plan subsurface exploration.
key_points: Preliminary design begins with terrain reconnaissance and office study
Key information sources: USGS topographic and geologic maps, USDA soil surveys, well logs, air photos
Construction records from nearby structures are increasingly valuable in congested areas
Review historical SPT data with judgment regarding reliability of older drilling methods
Terrain reconnaissance focuses on geologic and geomorphic features at the project site
Field reconnaissance should involve the bridge engineer and design team members
sections.applicability: Planning and scoping geotechnical investigations for shallow foundation projects.

sections.title: Field Reconnaissance
sections.summary: Site reconnaissance with the bridge engineer and design team assesses foundation conditions and guides foundation type selection. Tasks include visual assessment of nearby structures for settlement evidence, surface geology and geomorphology review, inspection of water crossings for scour, utility and obstruction identification, and site access assessment. A subsurface exploration plan or terrain reconnaissance report should be prepared upon completion.
sections.body: (pp. 30-31) The area concept of site exploration allows the geotechnical engineer to extend results from a limited number of explorations to the entire geologic deposit, reducing subsurface exploration costs. Application requires proper equipment and techniques under the direction of a knowledgeable geotechnical engineer. A site reconnaissance with the bridge engineer and design team is recommended to assess foundation conditions and foundation type selection. The field reconnaissance should include: visual assessment of nearby structures and their foundation performance; assessment of surface geology and geomorphology (slope instability, rock outcrops, erosion); inspection of water crossings for scour evidence; location of existing structures or abandoned foundations; location of subsurface and overhead utilities; and assessment of site access for exploration equipment. Upon completion, the geotechnical engineer should prepare a subsurface exploration plan or terrain reconnaissance report.
key_points: Area concept extends limited exploration results to the entire geologic deposit
Site reconnaissance with bridge engineer and design team is recommended
Assess nearby structures for foundation performance and settlement evidence
Inspect water crossings for scour evidence and streambed materials
Identify existing structures, abandoned foundations, and utilities that may affect new foundations
Prepare a subsurface exploration plan or terrain reconnaissance report upon completion
Exploration plan should outline site suitability, proposed locations, expected conditions, and cost estimates
sections.applicability: Planning field investigations and site visits for shallow foundation design projects.

sections.title: Subsurface Explorations and In Situ Testing
sections.summary: The subsurface exploration program depends on design objectives, expected soil conditions, and foundation type. For shallow foundations, scope and sampling differ from deep foundation investigations. SPT is the minimum level of in situ testing; CPT, PMT, and DMT provide supplemental information. Minimum exploration levels are defined in NHI (Cheney & Chassie 2000) and AASHTO (1988) references.
sections.body: (p. 32) The procedures employed in a subsurface exploration program depend on project design objectives, expected site soil conditions, and the type of foundation being considered. For shallow foundations, the extent, location, and sampling of subsurface materials will differ from deep foundation investigations. The minimum level of subsurface exploration and sampling is discussed in the Soils and Foundations Workshop Reference Manual (Cheney & Chassie, 2000) and the Manual on Subsurface Investigations (AASHTO, 1988).
key_points: Exploration program depends on design objectives, expected soil conditions, and foundation type
Shallow foundation exploration differs from deep foundation investigation in extent and sampling
Minimum exploration and sampling levels are defined in FHWA and AASHTO references
sections.applicability: General guidance on planning subsurface exploration programs for shallow foundations.

sections.title: Standard Penetration Test
sections.summary: SPT (AASHTO T-206/ASTM D-1586): 63-kg hammer, 0.76 m drop; N-value = blows for second and third 150-mm increments. Table 4-1 correlates N with relative density (sands) and consistency (clays). Figures 4-1 and 4-2 relate N to relative density and friction angle. Hammer efficiency correction: N60 = (ER/60%) × N_field (Eq 4-1); automatic hammers typically 70–90% efficient.
sections.body: (pp. 32-35) The Standard Penetration Test (SPT) is the most widely used field test in the United States, standardized by AASHTO T-206 and ASTM D-1586. The test consists of driving a split-spoon sampler 0.46 m (18 in) with the 63-kg (140-lb) hammer falling through a drop of 0.76 m (30 in). The first 150-mm (6-in) increment is the seating load; the sum of the next two 150-mm increments is the Standard Penetration Value (N). N-values indicate relative density of cohesionless soils and consistency of cohesive soils as correlated in Table 4-1. SPT N-values are also used to estimate strength and compressibility of granular soils through correlations in Figures 4-1 and 4-2, which relate N-value to relative density and friction angle. If a hammer system other than a rope and cathead with 60% efficiency is used, the N-value should be corrected using Equation 4-1.
key_points: SPT standardized by AASHTO T-206 and ASTM D-1586
63-kg hammer, 0.76 m drop; N-value = sum of blows for second and third 150-mm increments
N-values correlate with relative density (sands) and consistency (clays) per Table 4-1
Figures 4-1 and 4-2 relate N-value to relative density and friction angle for granular soils
Figure 4-1 is a function of both N-value and effective overburden stress; do not correct N for overburden
Hammer efficiency correction: N60 = (ER/60%) * N_field (Equation 4-1)
Automatic hammers typically have 70-90% efficiency; 80% commonly assumed
Correlations for gravels and clays from SPT are relatively unreliable
equations: Eq. 4-1: N60 = (ER / 60%)(N_FIELD); N60 = SPT N-value corrected for hammer efficiency; ER = Energy Ratio, the efficiency or percent of theoretical free fall energy delivered by the hammer system actually used; N_FIELD = blowcount recorded in the field. Example: ER = 80%, N_FIELD = 30 gives N60 = 40 (p. 33)
figures: Figure 4-1: Correlation Between Relative Density and SPT Resistance (NAVFAC, 1986a, after Gibbs & Holtz) (p. 34)
Figure 4-2: Correlation Between Relative Density, Material Classification and Angle of Internal Friction for Coarse-Grained Soils (NAVFAC, 1986a) (p. 35)
tables: Table 4-1: Soil Properties Correlated with Standard Penetration Test Values. Sands (reliable), N: 0-4 very loose, 4-10 loose, 10-30 medium, 30-50 dense, over 50 very dense. Clays (relatively unreliable), N: below 2 very soft, 2-4 soft, 4-8 medium, 8-15 stiff, 15-30 very stiff, over 30 hard (p. 33)
sections.applicability: SPT testing procedures, N-value correlations, and hammer efficiency corrections for foundation design.

sections.title: Subsurface Exploration Program
sections.summary: Minimum program: one drill hole per pier or abutment element, staggered at opposite ends; boring termination at N ≥ 20 for 6 continuous meters or 3 m into rock with ≥50% core recovery. Split-spoon samples at 1.5-m intervals (0.75-m within 4.5 m of bearing elevation); undisturbed tube samples in cohesive soils. CPT may supplement but should not replace borings at bridge sites.
sections.body: (pp. 35-37) A 65-mm (2-1/2-in.) boring costs less than one 0.3-m (12-in.) pile, yet what it shows may allow shallow foundations and the elimination of all piles. No rigid rules fix the number, depth, spacing and character of tests; the program must give the strength and compressibility of the soils within the foundation's zone of influence, with site-specific data at each pier, abutment and retaining wall on material type, density or consistency, and ground water. Its scale depends on the structure's importance and criticality, the loading, the budget and the schedule. The minimum program for a typical structure site (soft ground may need undisturbed samples or in situ tests): (1) at least one drill hole at each pier or abutment over 9 m (30 ft) long, staggered at opposite ends of adjacent footings, and one at each extremity of piers or abutments over 9 m (100 ft) (as printed); drilled with techniques that allow standard in situ tests in a stable hole (mud rotary with or without casing, continuous flight augers); CPT may substitute for borings but should not be the only data at a bridge site (not for very dense soils or cobbles and boulders; no samples, so no classification; but near-continuous layering); (2) estimate the boring depth from the reconnaissance, past the depth of influence (Section 3.1.5) unless rock comes first, with minimum criteria such as termination after SPT resistance of 20 blows per 0.3 m (1 ft) for 6 continuous m (20 ft), or 3 m (10 ft) into rock with average recovery of 50 percent or more, set from local design requirements and conditions, and more stringent where high lateral loads (impact, seismic) may act; (3) split-spoon samples at 1.5-m (5-ft) intervals or at changes in material, and at 0.75-m (2-1/2-ft) intervals for at least 4.5 m (15 ft) below a possible footing elevation on natural soil (disturbed, for index tests only); undisturbed tube samples at 1.5-m (5-ft) intervals in at least one boring in cohesive soils, at 3 m (10 ft) for cohesive deposits deeper than 9 m (30 ft); vane shear tests at 1.5- to 3-m (5- to 10-ft) intervals in soft clay; (4) record SPT data per ASTM D-1586; (5) rough visual description by the crew, split-spoon samples sealed in plastic bags and jars, tube samples sealed and stored upright in a shockproof insulated box; (6) record water levels: seepage or artesian pressure during drilling (head above ground measured by extending casing until flow stops), at the end of each day and at completion, and at least 24 hours after completion; water used in drilling can give a false level, and clays may need more than 1 week, so complete the boring as a piezometer. Open-end rod driving without samples, or water levels read after the last sample was removed, should be discouraged; good driller-engineer communication is essential.
key_points: A 65-mm boring costs less than one 0.3-m pile and may allow elimination of all piles
At least one drill hole at each pier or abutment over 9 m (30 ft) long, staggered; one at each extremity of elements over '9 m (100 ft)' as printed
Borings past the depth of influence; e.g., stop after N >= 20 blows/0.3 m for 6 continuous m (20 ft), or 3 m (10 ft) into rock with average recovery >= 50%
More stringent termination criteria where high lateral loads (impact, seismic) may act
Split-spoon samples at 1.5-m intervals; 0.75-m intervals for at least 4.5 m below a possible footing elevation
Tube samples at 1.5-m intervals in at least one boring in cohesive soils (3 m in deposits deeper than 9 m); vane shear at 1.5-3 m in soft clay
Water levels: during drilling, end of each day, at completion and 24 hours after; clays may need over 1 week (piezometer)
CPT may substitute for borings but should not be the only data at a bridge site
sections.applicability: Designing a subsurface exploration program for shallow foundation investigations.

sections.title: In Situ Testing
sections.summary: SPT is the minimum in situ testing for shallow foundation design. CPT provides nearly continuous data and better soil layering definition but cannot penetrate dense soils or cobbles and requires empirical correlations. PMT and DMT measure in situ stress-strain properties; a PMT-based settlement prediction method (Briaud and colleagues) has potential for ordinary working loads and higher transient loads such as earthquake or ice (Section 5.3.4.3).
sections.body: (p. 38) The SPT is considered the minimum level of in situ testing for foundation design. The cone penetration test (CPT) is the next most common, offering nearly continuous data as the probe is pushed into the ground, providing more discrete and accurate soil layering definition than split-spoon sampling at 1.5-m intervals. CPT limitations include inability to penetrate very dense soils or cobbles/boulders, no sample recovery, and reliance on empirical correlations. The pressuremeter test (PMT) and flat dilatometer test (DMT) can measure stress-strain properties in situ and have been used to predict shallow foundation performance. Recent research by Briaud and colleagues has resulted in a new method of predicting shallow foundation settlement as a function of applied load based on PMT data, which has potential for improving settlement prediction under ordinary working loads and under higher transient loads such as earthquake or ice loads (Section 5.3.4.3). References: ASTM 3441 and Briaud & Miran (printed 'Riaund & Miran'), 1992, for the CPT and dilatometer; Briaud (1989) for the pressuremeter.
key_points: SPT is the minimum level of in situ testing for foundation design
CPT provides nearly continuous data and better soil layer definition than SPT
CPT limitations: cannot penetrate very dense soils or cobbles, no sample recovery, empirical correlations
CPT should supplement, not replace, borings at bridge sites
Pressuremeter (PMT) and dilatometer (DMT) measure in situ stress-strain properties
PMT-based settlement prediction (Briaud & Gibbens 1994, 1995; Briaud et al. 2000) has potential for working and transient loads
sections.applicability: Selection and application of in situ testing methods for shallow foundation design.

sections.title: Rock and IGM Mass Characterization
sections.summary: Rock and IGM masses require evaluation of lithology, strength (qu, c, phi), deformability (E, nu), RQD, and discontinuity frequency, orientation, aperture, and condition relative to foundation width. Table 4-2 summarizes applicable in situ and laboratory tests. Design recommendations typically rely on rock type, core recovery, RQD, and unconfined compressive strength combined with local geological knowledge and engineering judgment.
sections.body: (pp. 38-39) A natural rock or intermediate geomaterial (IGM) mass is rarely a continuous, isotropic, homogeneous material. A rock mass is composed of intact or weathered blocks separated by discontinuities (joints, bedding planes, sheared zones, faults). Important characteristics for shallow foundation design on rock include: lithology, IGM genesis, strength properties (qu, c, phi), deformation properties (E, nu), frequency and spacing of discontinuities (especially relative to foundation width), orientation (strike and dip), aperture and condition of discontinuities, degree of weathering, and groundwater condition. Exploration methods include field reconnaissance, geological mapping, drilling/coring, test excavation, in situ testing, geophysical methods, field load testing, and laboratory testing (Table 4-2). Design recommendations for footings on rock or IGM are commonly based on limited data: rock type, core description, core recovery percentage, RQD values, and unconfined compressive strength, combined with local geological knowledge and engineering judgment.
key_points: Rock and IGM masses are rarely continuous, isotropic, or homogeneous
Key characterization parameters: lithology, strength (qu, c, phi), deformability (E, nu), RQD
Discontinuity properties (frequency, spacing, orientation, aperture, condition) are critical
Spacing of discontinuities relative to foundation width is especially important
Table 4-2 summarizes in situ and laboratory tests for footings on rock or IGMs
Some tests are for stronger materials (borehole jacking, unconfined compression); others for weaker IGMs (PMT, DMT)
Design recommendations often based on limited data combined with local knowledge and judgment
tables: Table 4-2: Summary of Commonly Used In Situ and Laboratory Testing for Footings on Rock or IGMs (after Arman et al., 1997) (p. 40)
sections.applicability: Characterizing rock and IGM foundations for shallow foundation design.

sections.title: Laboratory Testing
sections.summary: Laboratory tests must reproduce the field stress conditions, moisture states and load paths. Cohesionless soils can often be designed from SPT-based strength and compressibility correlations. For cohesive soils, which can be weak and compressible in ways SPT N-values do not show, consolidation testing is usually essential for settlement and shear-strength testing should be considered where a bearing failure could develop. Phase relationships, effective stress and overburden stress are reviewed.
sections.body: (pp. 39-40) A useful laboratory testing program requires testing soil samples under conditions that exist in the ground or that will occur as a result of construction and loading. The stress conditions, moisture states, and load paths imposed on the representative soil sample should match field conditions. The basic concepts of laboratory testing for strength and deformation characteristics are reviewed, beginning with phase relationships, effective stress, and overburden stress, then common laboratory tests for shear strength and compressibility.
key_points: Laboratory tests should simulate in situ stress conditions and anticipated loading
Stress conditions, moisture states, and load paths should match field conditions
Basic concepts reviewed: phase relationships, effective stress, overburden stress
Cohesionless soils can often be designed using SPT-based strength and compressibility correlations
Cohesive soils: consolidation testing usually essential; shear-strength testing considered if a bearing failure could develop (p. 46)
sections.applicability: General guidance on laboratory testing programs for shallow foundation design.

sections.title: Phase and Volume Relationships
sections.summary: Soil is a three-phase material (solid, water, gas). Table 4-3 provides Eqs 4-2 through 4-20 relating unit weight, void ratio (e), porosity (n), water content (w), degree of saturation (S), and specific gravity (Gs). Void ratio is a general indicator of relative strength and compressibility. Consolidation occurs as excess pore-water pressure dissipates over time in low-permeability soils.
sections.body: (pp. 40-43) Soil is a three-phase material (solid, water, gas) whose weight and volume depend on specific gravity, void/pore space size, and degree of saturation. The phase relation block diagram (Figure 4-3) shows volume components (V_A air, V_W water, V_S solids) and weight components (W_W water, W_S solids). Table 4-3 summarizes the weight-volume relationships, dimensionless ratios, and functional relationships (Equations 4-2 through 4-20). Of particular note is the void ratio, e, which is a general indicator of relative strength and compressibility: low void ratios indicate strong, incompressible soils, and high void ratios may indicate weak, compressible soils. Deformation under load depends on intergranular forces and the amount of pore water. In saturated soils with low permeability, load is initially carried by pore water (excess pore-water pressure), which dissipates over time as water is expelled and soil particles accept the load -- this process is consolidation.
key_points: Soil is a three-phase material: solid, water, gas (air)
Phase relationships defined by specific gravity, void space, and degree of saturation
Void ratio (e) is a general indicator of relative strength and compressibility
Low void ratio indicates strong, incompressible soils; high void ratio indicates weak, compressible soils
Table 4-3 contains Equations 4-2 through 4-20 for all weight-volume and functional relationships
Consolidation occurs as excess pore-water pressure dissipates and intergranular stress increases
Spring analogy (Figure 4-4) explains consolidation: valve = permeability, spring = soil skeleton, water = pore fluid
equations: Eq. 4-2: gamma = W / V, unit weight (general definition); W = weight (force F); V = volume (L^3) (p. 42)
Eq. 4-3: gamma_sat = W / V, unit weight of saturated soil (p. 42)
Eq. 4-4: gamma_S = W_S / V_S, unit weight of soil solids (p. 42)
Eq. 4-5: gamma_w = W_W / V_W = 9.8 kN/m3 (62.4 pcf), unit weight of water (p. 42)
Eq. 4-6: gamma_d = W_S / V, dry unit weight (weight of solids only over the total volume) (p. 42)
Eq. 4-7: gamma' = W' / V, buoyant (submerged) unit weight; W' = buoyant weight of the soil mass on complete submergence, W' = W - gamma_w V (p. 42)
Eq. 4-8: gamma' = gamma_sat - gamma_w (p. 42)
Eq. 4-9: G_S = gamma_S / gamma_W, specific gravity of soil solids (p. 42)
Eq. 4-10: e = V_V / V_S, void ratio (void vs. solid volume) (p. 42)
Eq. 4-11: n = V_V / V, porosity (void vs. total volume) (p. 42)
Eq. 4-12: w = W_W / W_S, water content (water vs. solid weight) (p. 42)
Eq. 4-13: S = V_W / V_V, degree of saturation (p. 42)
Eq. 4-16: gamma = (G_S + Se) gamma_W / (1 + e) (p. 42)
Eq. 4-17: gamma_d = G_S gamma_W / (1 + e) (p. 42)
Eq. 4-18: gamma_d = gamma / (1 + w) (p. 42)
Eq. 4-20: gamma' = (G_S - 1) gamma_W / (1 + e) (p. 42)
figures: Figure 4-4: Spring Analogy as Applied to Consolidation (Holtz and Kovacs, 1981) (p. 43)
tables: Table 4-3: Weight-Volume Relationships, Dimensionless Ratios and Functional Relationships (Eqs. 4-2 to 4-20) (p. 42)
sections.applicability: Fundamental soil phase relationships and weight-volume computations for geotechnical design.

sections.title: Principle of Effective Stress
sections.summary: Effective stress (Eq 4-21: σ' = σ – u) is the intergranular stress that resists shearing and controls compression; pore-water pressure has no shear strength. In saturated clay loaded quickly, pore pressure initially carries the entire applied load. As pore pressure dissipates over time, effective stress increases and consolidation settlement occurs.
sections.body: (p. 44) Under an applied load, the total stress in a saturated soil sample is composed of pore-water pressure (neutral stress, acting equally in all directions in both water and soil) and effective stress (intergranular stress, acting at soil particle contacts). Because pore water has no shear strength, only the effective stress is effective in resisting shearing or limiting compression. The effective stress equals the total stress minus the pore water pressure (Equation 4-21). Changes in effective stress control the volumetric strain in a soil. In the oedometer test (Figure 4-5), when a saturated clay is loaded quickly, essentially zero volume change occurs initially as pore pressure increases. Over time, excess pore pressure dissipates as water drains through porous stones, and the effective stress increases to equal the new total stress.
key_points: Total stress = pore-water pressure + effective stress (Equation 4-21: sigma' = sigma - u)
Pore-water pressure acts equally in all directions and has no shear strength
Only effective (intergranular) stress resists shearing and controls compression
Changes in effective stress control volumetric strain development
In saturated clay loaded quickly, pore pressure initially carries the entire applied load
Over time, excess pore pressure dissipates and effective stress increases (consolidation)
Oedometer test (Figure 4-5) demonstrates this principle in the laboratory
equations: Eq. 4-21: sigma' = sigma - u; sigma = total stress; u = pore water pressure; sigma' = effective stress (p. 44)
figures: Figure 4-5: Conceptual Arrangement of Laboratory Oedometer Test (p. 44)
sections.applicability: Fundamental principle governing soil strength, compressibility, and consolidation behavior.

sections.title: Overburden Stress
sections.summary: Total overburden stress is computed by summing (unit weight × layer thickness) for all layers above a point. Effective stress equals total stress minus pore-water pressure (depth below water table × 9.81 kN/m³). Stress profiles should extend to about 2B below the bearing elevation in 0.5B increments. Profiles are used throughout shallow foundation design and for specifying laboratory test starting conditions.
sections.body: (pp. 45-46) The weight of overlying soil exerts an overburden stress that is a function of unit weight and depth. When conducting laboratory tests on soil samples, it is important to reestablish the in situ stress state that existed prior to sampling. The total overburden stress is computed by summing the product of total unit weight and layer thickness for each stratigraphic layer. A 5-step procedure for constructing stress profiles: (1) Divide the subsurface into layers based on soil stratigraphy, classification, groundwater table, and unit weight changes, using increments of about half the footing width for twice the footing width below bearing depth; (2) Determine total vertical stress at each depth by multiplying unit weight by layer thickness and summing; (3) Determine pore water pressure below the water table by multiplying depth below water table by gamma_w (9.81 kN/m^3); (4) Calculate effective stress by subtracting pore water pressure from total stress; (5) Plot total and effective stresses versus depth or elevation.
key_points: Overburden stress is a function of unit weight of overlying soil and depth
Laboratory tests require reestablishing in situ stress state as starting condition
Total overburden stress = sum of (unit weight * layer thickness) for all layers above the point
Pore water pressure = depth below water table * gamma_w (9.81 kN/m^3 = 62.4 pcf)
Effective stress = total stress - pore water pressure (below water table)
Stress profile should extend to about 2B below the bearing depth using 0.5B layer increments
Unit weight may be determined from undisturbed samples or estimated from SPT N-values and descriptions
Stress profiles are used throughout shallow foundation design and for specifying lab test starting conditions
sections.applicability: Computing overburden stress profiles for use in shallow foundation design and laboratory test specification.
